questions.knowledge_point: Finding Areas Bounded by Other Polar Curves
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14066449/assets/c06da8f06e8d640c23dbd81885fdd1bd5e5d89b15b1729cacd82ac52f301e44d.png)

Find the area bounded by the polar curve $r={e}^{3\theta }$ for $0\le \theta \le 2\pi ,$ as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )={e}^{3\theta }$, ${\theta }_{1}=0$ and ${\theta }_{2}=2\pi $, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{({e}^{3\theta })}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{e}^{6\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{6}{e}^{6\theta }{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{12}({e}^{12\pi }-{e}^{0}) \\  & =\frac{1}{12}({e}^{12\pi }-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Find the area bounded by the polar curve $r={e}^{\theta +1}$ for $0\le \theta \le \pi ,$ as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )={e}^{\theta +1}$, ${\theta }_{1}=0$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\pi $, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{({e}^{\theta +1})}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{e}^{2\theta +2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2\theta +2}{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{4}({e}^{2\pi +2}-{e}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{e}^{2}({e}^{2\pi }-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Find the area $A$ bounded by the polar curve $r=4-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ for $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4},$ as shown above. Do not round the answer.

$A=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=4-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, ${\theta }_{1}=-\frac{\pi }{4}$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{4}$, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}(4-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}(16-16\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}(16-16\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(18\theta +16\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )){|}_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(18\theta \,{|}_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}+16\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{|}_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,{|}_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}) \\  & =9\theta \,{|}_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}+8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{|}_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,{|}_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4} \\  & =9(\frac{\pi }{4}+\frac{\pi }{4})+8(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{4}))-\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =\frac{9\pi }{2}+8(0)-\frac{1}{2}(2) \\  & =\frac{9\pi }{2}-1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding Areas Bounded by Other Polar Curves
questions.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

When $r(\theta )=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $, ${\theta }_{1}=0$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{4}$, this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}({sin}^{2}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}(1+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\theta -\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}{2}){|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{\pi }{4}+\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{\pi +2}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Area Bounded by the Loop of a Limaçon
questions.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=1+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, ${\theta }_{1}=-\frac{\pi }{2}$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}$, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(1+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(1+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}(\frac{3}{2}+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{3}{2}\theta -2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{4}){|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{3}{2}\theta \,{|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{4}\,{|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\,) \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\theta \,{|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,{|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{8}\,{|}_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}(\frac{\pi }{2}+\frac{\pi }{2})-(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2}))-\frac{1}{8}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi )) \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}-(0-0)-0 \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$
